data.content: I'd ban them in classrooms, not in schoolbags. The evidence on distraction is strong: phones fragment attention, and the kids who struggle most lose the most. But a blanket ban ignores the asthma inhaler reminder, the diabetic glucose monitor, the kid texting a parent about pickup. So: bell-to-bell limits, clear carve-outs for medical and accessibility needs, and teach digital judgement rather than pretend the devices don't exist. The question isn't whether phones distract. It's whether prohibition teaches anything.

data.content: Ban, plainly defined: no pupil-operated smartphone during instructional hours. My case rests on three reasons. First, a school is a compelled audience; the child beside you did not consent to your feed, and the state may regulate speech in a nonpublic forum. Second, enforcement asymmetry: we already ban calculators, notes and pagers, yet we flinch only at the one device with infinite reach. Third, the counterfactual is not measured either, so put the distractions, the sleep debt and the savings from doing something on one ledger. Define your terms, then count.

retrieved.text:
Moot court notes: "This house would adopt a nationwide four-day work week" V. Hale, for the Meridian Bar Society exhibition debate. Private notes.

¶ 1. Expect the opposition to say the evidence base is narrow. Concede scope early, then shift the burden: the status quo is also a policy and has to justify itself.

¶ 2. Historical anchor: the Meridian Working Hours Act 1931 made the two-day weekend the default. It gave agriculture and shipping a ten-year transition and exempted continuous services.

¶ 3. Continuous-coverage sectors already run on shift rules under Part IV of the Working Time Code: rest periods, a cap on consecutive shifts, and averaging over a reference period. A shorter standard week sits inside that structure.

¶ 4. Phase-in precedent: sector-by-sector timetables, collective agreements first, the public sector as model employer. Courts have upheld staged duties where the end point is clear.

recalled.text: Victor argued that nationwide means a statutory default week with a transition, not an identical schedule, citing the Working Hours Act 1931 as precedent for phasing and continuous-service exemptions.
Victor closed that the motion already contains sequencing: set the default, exempt continuous services explicitly, phase by sector, and mandate measurement.
Victor argued the status quo also runs unmeasured, so both the mandate's cost and the saving from doing nothing belong on the same ledger.
Victor conceded Mei's 18-27% staffed-hours premium across nine continuous-coverage operations was real and measured where coverage was held constant.

data.content: Banning phones in schools is a working-time question wearing a discipline costume. My evidence, not my gut: shift-based organisations holding coverage constant needed 18% to 27% more staffed hours when they shortened the working week, and only two clawed any back. Teachers aren't exempt; enforcement is real labour, and someone pays. Second-order: the pupils who suffer most from phones are often the ones with the least supervision at home, so a ban redistributes their supervision costs onto schools. I favour a middle path: light-touch rules, exemptions for accessibility and medical need, measured before mandated.

recalled.text: Mei closed urging sequence, explicit exemption of continuous services, and mandated measurement before a nationwide default, calling Amara's ward result good but untested for round-the-clock cover.
Mei cited nine shift-based organisations holding coverage constant that needed 18% to 27% more staffed hours on a shorter week; two clawed part back within six months, seven did not measure it.
Mei argued the pilots covered no hospitals, transport operators or care homes, and fewer than half the firms measured output consistently, so the gains were partly redistributed rather than created.
Mei conceded the status-quo-is-also-a-policy line lands and that doing nothing costs money in absence, agency fees and resignations.

data.content: What's still open is measurement, and that's why I'd land where I did. Amara's carve-outs are good but untested for round-the-clock cover, and Victor's ledger counts what he can see. My concession stands: doing nothing is also a policy, and absence and resignations cost money. But a mandate built on one ward's result, with fewer than half the pilots measuring output consistently, is a bet, not evidence. Define it, exempt continuous services, then count — otherwise you're redistributing, not creating, the gains.

So my closing is this. Ban phones from instruction, not from children's pockets, with medical and accessibility carve-outs written in and measured. Victor's ledger counts what he can see; the parent waiting on a pickup text can't be legislated invisible. Define it, exempt need, then count. That's the stronger bet than prohibition by assertion.

data.content: What remains open is sequencing, and sequencing is precisely what defeats the objection. Your carve-outs are answerable in text: the medical device and the pickup call sit outside the ban, named and exempted. Your measurement gap is answerable in time: phase by year group, publish the baseline, sunset the rule if the ledger does not move. That is not prohibition by assertion; that is a mandate with a return path. Mei calls it a bet. I call it the only wager on the table that ever gets counted. Absentia rei non est probatio.
